title: Backrooms Hill
solution: Swapping a_i and a_{i+2} lets values at odd positions be permuted arbitrarily among odd positions, and likewise for even positions, so each value v has a fixed position-parity class c(v) and the question is whether some hill places every value on a position of its class. Build any hill by taking values in decreasing order: the maximum sits at the peak p, and each next value extends the occupied interval either one step left or one step right. Fix the parity P of p (the maximum's class must equal P). When the j-th largest value is placed after L left-extensions so far, the left slot is p-L-1 and the right slot is p+j-L, so the parity of each slot depends only on P, j and L mod 2. Run a DP over the values with state L mod 2 (a 2x2 reachability set) and accept if the final left count satisfies L_total+1 ≡ P, because then p = L_total+1 is consistent. This is O(n log n) for the sort (O(n) with counting since values are 1..n) per test.

rejected_patterns.reason: The 2-state DP is correct but collapses to a deterministic check: at odd steps both frontier slots share a parity, at even steps exactly one fits. So the whole test is: sort values descending, each consecutive pair (1st,2nd),(3rd,4th),... must come from different index-parity classes, and when n is odd the smallest value must be in the odd-position (1-indexed) class. Verified against brute force on 3000 random arrays. Nobody searching DP should land here.
No greedy choice or exchange argument. Once values are ordered, the placement is forced by parity.
This is a yes/no decision problem with no construction to output. Growing the hill outward from the peak is only part of the reasoning.

added_patterns.reason: The core structure is ordering values by size: in a hill the top-j values fill a contiguous block around the peak, so the check pairs consecutive values in sorted order (a counting sort works because values are 1..n).

rejected_tags.reason: same as pattern: the DP collapses to a pairwise parity check

notes.solver: Key insight is the parity invariant (distance-2 swaps preserve index parity, and odd/even classes are freely permutable). The core check is a tiny-state DP over values in decreasing order (peak parity x left-count parity); an editorial likely phrases it as a greedy/case analysis on how the parity classes of sorted values alternate (placing the largest values outward from the peak), so greedy/constructive are listed with lower confidence. Not interval-dp: although the occupied interval grows, only parities matter, so the state is O(1). Sorting is scaffolding (values are a permutation of 1..n). verified_on_samples detail is duplicated in verified_on_samples_note because the key must be boolean.
notes.skeptic: Proposal's DP reproduces all 7 samples and matches brute force (independently re-checked, n<=8). Simpler equivalent solution, verified against the DP on 3000 random arrays with n<=9: map each value to the parity of its index, sort descending, require vs[2i] and vs[2i+1] to differ in parity for every full pair, and if n is odd require the minimum's parity to be odd-position (1-indexed), since the minimum must sit at an end and both ends are odd positions. Only parity-argument and sorting are central. Summary is accurate at about 55 words, so it is unchanged.
